newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND BANK SEEN ALLOWING FIRMER MARKKA -ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND BANK SEEN ALLOWING FIRMER MARKKA -ANALYSTS.

text.p: The Bank of Finland said on Monday that inflation threatened to speed up and it would act to prevent that, and also indicated it might let the markka firm and move away from its ERM central parity, analysts said.

Short-term interest rates rose and the markka jumped against the German mark on the news, which some market economists said marked a shift from the central bank's earlier assessment that inflation was well under control despite heady economic growth.
But views were mixed on whether the message signalled that a monetary policy tightening was in the cards alredy this year.
"The Bank of Finland clearly indicated that ... they feel inflation pressures have become significantly higher," said Esko Torsti, head of market advisory at S-E Banken here.

"This was the first warning, maybe there will be a second warning, maybe not, but in any case the time for the next tightening is drawing reasonably close," he said, adding he now believed monetary policy would be tightened this year.
A rate hike was now more likely to come in the third quarter rather than maybe at the earliest in the final quarter as S-E Banken had forecast until now, he said.
Releasing the 2/1997 issue of its quarterly Markka & Talous (Markka and the Economy) publication, the Bank of Finland said the risks of accelerating inflation had increased.

It expected underlying inflation to accelerate to slightly over two percent in 1998 compared to a stated monetary policy target for a core inflation rate of no more than around two percent year-on-year.

"While the current outlook does not portend a change in the stance of monetary policy, an increase in the probability that inflation will exceed the forecasted rate would force the central bank to consider monetary tightening," it said.

Kirsi Hokka, chief economist at Handelsbanken Markets Finland said: "I still don't believe that it (a key rate hike) will come before the turn of the year ... but that does not mean that a tightening would be ruled out,"

The central bank's view that risks of accelerating inflation had increased was a "natural response" to the Paper Workers' Union's announcement last week that it would not join a centralised nation-wide incomes settlement, she said.
Charlotte Kamp, analyst at Den Danske Bank in Copenhagen, said she saw no reason for a Finnish rate hike until 1998 "if the pay talks go smoothly."
But the bank may act pre-emptively as it has before, she added.
Petteri Hirvonen, chief economist at brokerage Davy Protos, said a key rate hike could come in the autumn in connection with the incomes settlement talks, or afterwards.
The central bank's view that it would not change its monetary policy stance now meant that it would have to wait for more information before acting.
Anticipating higher official interest rates, market rates rose and the markka strengthened in the afternoon. The markka would remain under pressure to gain further, the analysts said.

"My interpretation is that they are willing to take the risk that the markka's exchange rate against the German mark will stray quite far away, maybe even 10 penni (3.3 percent), from its ERM central parity," Torsti said.
The markka's central parity in the European exchange rate mechanism is 3.04 per mark.
Hokka underlined that monetary policy could be tightened as well by raising interest rates as by allowing the currency to strengthen.
The consensus view on financial markets has been that the central bank wants to keep the markka near its ERM midpoint.
